sections.synopsis: A frontal system continues to move east into the Cascades into tonight. A warm front will boost temperatures as it moves northwards Saturday for brief dry conditions. A potent cold front brings rain and gusty winds Saturday night into Sunday. The active pattern continues at times into next week.
sections.short_term:
A front continues to slowly slide southeast this afternoon, leading to lingering steadier rain across the southern tier of western Washington. South winds are also slowly tapering off. Peak wind gusts over the last 12 hours generally reached 40 to 60 MPH along the coast, and from Admiralty Inlet northwards. The front will progress east of the Cascades into tonight, resulting in generally drier conditions and lighter winds. A warm front then lifts northwards into Saturday. Although the majority of western Washington will be dry into the afternoon, rain may continue at times along the western Olympic Peninsula. Temperatures will peak in the 60s on Saturday as well in the warm sector.

A potent cold front progresses eastwards Saturday evening into Saturday night across W WA. This will bring a period of steadier rainfall, with rain rates briefly reaching 0.15-0.25" per hour along the front. The more impactful aspect to this system will be the stronger southerly winds associated with the front. Latest REFS guidance suggests a 50-75% chance of gusts exceeding 58 MPH later Saturday (High Wind Warning threshold), with a High Wind Watch remaining in effect. Additional wind headlines may be needed elsewhere with gusts ranging 30 to 45 MPH for most areas Saturday PM into early Sunday. Due to continued foliage on the trees for many locations, localized power outages will be possible. Furthermore, clogged storm drains may occur when the period of gusty winds overlaps with steadier rain Saturday evening. Give yourself extra time if traveling Saturday evening.

Steadier rain transitions to periodic showers on Sunday, with the majority of the QPF focused on the North Cascades and Olympics. Snow levels around 7500 feet through Saturday night fall to near 4500 feet on Sunday for high elevation mountain snowfall. By Sunday, the primary concern shifts to high surf conditions along the coast. Seas build to 20 to 28 feet on Sunday, resulting in large breaking waves along the coast. A High Surf Advisory has been issued, and will need to monitor the need for a High Surf Warning over the next day as periods approach 15 to 17 seconds. Caution should be used when in or near the water, especially those who will be participating in razor clam digging. High temperatures cool into the 50s by Sunday.
sections.long_term: A brief shortwave ridge builds over the Pacific Northwest Sunday night into Monday for drier conditions. The next warm front quickly approaches Monday afternoon for additional rain and locally breezy conditions late Monday through Monday night. Ensembles suggest a steady plume of moisture then becomes focused over Vancouver Island and Western Washington on Tuesday for additional rainfall, warmer temperatures, and breezy conditions. At this time the heaviest QPF amounts are focused over the Olympics and North Cascades. Uncertainty increases on Wednesday as ridging builds over the interior Rockies with troughing offshore. This will continue to result in continued warmer temperatures, with the highest probability for rainfall over the Olympics. More widespread rainfall chances return Thursday into late week. JD
sections.marine:
An active marine pattern will continue into next week as a series of frontal systems impact area waters. A frontal system earlier today has brought elevated seas and winds. Seas will remain elevated above 10 feet and a Small Craft Advisory will follow once gale-force winds subside for the coastal waters and West Strait.

A stronger frontal system is expected Saturday afternoon into Sunday morning. This system will bring a plethora of hazards to area waters, including elevated seas and winds. With high-res guidance continuing to indicate a 70% chance or higher of seeing storm-force winds over the coastal waters, the Storm Watch has been upgraded to a Storm Warning. Gale Watches remain in effect for the interior waters. Seas are expected to build over 20 feet late Saturday night into Sunday, with seas building towards 28 feet in the outer coastal waters. Seas will gradually decrease towards Sunday night into Monday, but will remain above 10 feet.

Weak high pressure will briefly build over the waters on Monday. However, the next frontal system arrives in the evening, followed by multiple systems that will pose additional marine hazards to area waters.

sections.synopsis: A plume of moisture associated with now Tropical Storm Pena well south of the islands brought heavy rainfall to windward areas of the Big Island. While the deepest moisture has shifted off to the west, expect enhanced clouds and showers to continue into Saturday morning favoring Maui and Hawaii Counties. A second tropical disturbance will pass to the south of the state early next week, possibly enhancing shower activity to southern portions of the Big Island. The next best chance for increasing statewide shower chances arrives late next week.
sections.short_term:
Unsettled cloud bands shown on satellite east of the Hawaiian Islands are riding into the windward mountains on the breezy easterly trade winds. Expect continued periods of showers favoring windward mountain areas through the early Saturday morning hours.

We continue to see decreasing shower trends from Saturday into Sunday as a high pressure ridge north of the state increases downward vertical motions (subsidence), lowering and strengthening the trade wind subsidence temperature inversion. This lower and stronger temperature inversion around 6,000 to 7,000 feet elevation will cap vertical cloud growth and limit rainfall activity to brief passing showers mainly in the overnight to early morning hours over windward mountain areas.

No changes to the afternoon forecast grids this evening.
sections.marine:
Issued at 342 PM HST Fri Nov 6 2026 Fresh to strong trade winds with periods of near gales in the channels will prevail through the weekend as high pressure persists north of the state. A Small Craft Advisory (SCA) remains in place for all Hawaiian Waters due to a combination of winds and elevated seas through Saturday night. The SCA will likely remain in place through at least Sunday night as Tropical Storm Pena passes several hundred miles to the south and keeps the local pressure gradient tight. Winds are expected to ease slightly late Monday and Tuesday as the ridge to our north erodes and Pena moves away to the southwest. The SCA will likely be trimmed back to the typical windy waters around Big Island and Maui at that time. Trade winds are expected to strengthen again on Wednesday.

A north-northwest swell will continue a slow decline through Saturday, and surf along exposed north and west facing shores has fallen below High Surf Advisory thresholds. A reinforcing medium- period energy out of the north-northwest (325 to 340 degree) should arrive late Saturday into Sunday. Surf should reach advisory thresholds during the peak of the swell Sunday morning. Another large northwest to north-northwest swell is Wednesday or Thursday.

A small south-southwest swell should produce surf slightly above seasonal average through Saturday. A tiny pulse from the south- southeast may maintain south shore surf near seasonal average Sunday and Monday, followed by background level surf through the remainder of the week.

Rough surf along east-facing shores will hold around seasonal average through much of the week. Select northeast exposures should see long- period energy from the declining north-northwest swell into tonight.
